entities.name: Hassan II Mosque
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Hassan II Mosque in Casablanca, Morocco is the world's largest mosque outside of Mecca and Medina, completed in 1993 at a cost of $800 million. Designed by French architect Michel Pinseau and built over the Atlantic Ocean on a rocky promontory, it can accommodate 25,000 worshippers inside and 80,000 in the surrounding esplanade. Its 210-meter minaret — the world's tallest — is topped by a laser that points toward Mecca.

King Hassan II commissioned the mosque in 1980 to create a monument worthy of Morocco's millennium of Islamic civilization and to celebrate his 60th birthday. The project was funded through a national subscription, with Moroccans across all social classes contributing. Over 6,000 Moroccan artisans spent 7 years creating the mosque's hand-carved cedar ceilings, hand-laid marble floors, and intricate zellige tile work, making it the largest commission of traditional Moroccan craftsmanship in the modern era.

The mosque's most unusual feature is its glass floor over the ocean, fulfilling a Quranic verse about God's throne being built upon water. The retractable roof can open to allow the interior to be flooded with sunlight and ocean breezes. The complex includes a museum of Moroccan heritage, a library, a Quranic school, and ablution facilities for 20,000. Non-Muslim visitors are permitted for guided tours, a notable openness for a major mosque.
